Conclusion
This research examines the e ﬀects of tra ﬃc-induced
vibrations on historic structures in Ayutthaya Historical
Park by measurement of vibration waves and analysis
of the response of an ancient monument. The
expected outcome is to be bene ﬁcial for predicting
the intensity of tra ﬃc-induced ground motion and its
attenuation with distance from source. This can be
achieved by using basic information about soil layer
properties, speci ﬁcally the shear wave velocity. With
this information and the predicted level of ground
motion, it can be used to assess the potential impact
on ancient structures. A simple assessment can be
done by using ground motion criteria for historic struc-
tures such as the peak ground vibration. More detailed
assessments can be performed through dynamic
analysis of the structure, which can identify vulnerable
areas requiring protection against potential damage
caused by vibrations. In this work, attenuation of the
vibration waves traveling from sources was examined
for sites having di ﬀerent average shear wave velocities
of sediments. The attenuation in Ayutthaya is high due
to stiﬀ soils compared to other sites in the lower plains.
In general, attenuation tends to be more pronounced
for an increase in the shear wave velocity of sediments.
The observation in this study indicated that the
vibration intensity found in Ayutthaya Historical Park
was lower than the recommendations speciﬁ ed in
the international standard of vibration e ﬀect on the
historic structure and past research. The ﬁnite
element analysis of a model of an ancient stupa was
carried out for the detailed investigation. To create a
model, data from surveying the current condition of
the geometry and dynamic properties were used,
along with necessary parameters derived from a
review of past studies. This results in a model that
can accurately represent the dynamic behavior of the
stupa. From the analysis, the stress induced by
vibration was less than the strength of the ancient
brick-mortar system. Although the results reveal that
the eﬀects are not destructive to the ancient structures
at present, regular inspection and monitoring, and pro-
tection of those structures from long-term deterio-
ration caused by vibration and other environmental
eﬀects are indispensable.

To understand the vibration propagating away from
traﬃc sources and assess the e ﬀect on historical struc-
tures, this study conducted in situ measurements to
provide an empirical prediction of wave attenuation
at a site and performed dynamic analysis to examine
the response of structures. The basis of the investi-
gation is to measure ground vibration caused by
surface waves traveling from tra ﬃc sources using
several sensors placed along a line perpendicular to a
road. The attenuation rates are discussed with the dis-
tance from the road and the subsoil properties. Eﬀ ects
of vibration were assessed by comparing the peak par-
ticle velocities of ground records with the rec-
ommended criteria for historical structures. In
addition, a ﬁnite element analysis of an ancient stupa
in Ayutthaya subjected to ground vibrations was per-
formed to calculate the dynamic stress caused by
traﬃc.
Ayutthaya historical park
Ayutthaya Historical Park is located in Phra Nakhon Si
Ayutthaya province, Central Thailand. The Park has
been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since
1991 under criterion III as an excellent witness to the
period of development of a true national Thai art
(UNESCO). The Kingdom of Ayutthaya was established
as the capital city of Thailand in the period of 1350 –
1767 CE. During the era, the city developed greatly
and became one of the world ’s largest and most cos-
mopolitan urban areas. Buddhism highly ﬂourished
for several centuries and many monuments were
built in tribute to the Lord Buddha. However, the city
was abandoned after the war in 1767 CE. The cultural
monuments were left unmaintained and deteriorated
over time since then until the major restoration
carried out by the Fine Arts Department in 1956 and
1975. Recently, the city has been urbanized due to
tourism and economic expansions in past decades,
and the number of vehicles has greatly increased.
Therefore, the ancient historic structures in the park
have been more exposed to vibrations induced by
traﬃc.
Ayutthaya’s monument style was in ﬂuenced by
Sukhothai (the former Thai Kingdom), Sri Lanka, and
Khmer architecture. Most of the heritage remains in
Ayutthaya are bell-shaped masonry monuments
known as stupa,o r chedi in Thai. Figure 1 shows an
example of an ancient stupa of Wat Sam Pluem
located in the middle of a tra ﬃc-congested round-
about. Another tall stupa at the horizon in the ﬁgure
also well describes the Ayutthaya scene with many
monuments sparsely distributed in the city.
The long-term existence of these monuments could
be attributed to their robust structural system and resi-
lient materials. The Ayutthaya bell-shaped stupa fea-
tures a symmetrical, load-bearing structural system
with a large base area and a tapered upper cone-
shaped structure. The stresses in its elements resulting
from gravity loads are mostly in compression, which is
beneﬁcial for materials with low tensile strength, such
as brick and natural bonding materials. The stupa has
three main parts as can be seen in the example of
the drawing of Wat Sam Pluem in Figure 2 . The base
part is a multi-tiered, polygon shaped structure that
represents the Trailokya, a central concept in Bud-
dhism. The bell-shaped part in the middle is the relic
chamber of the stupa. The spire at the top serves as
a decorative element and signiﬁ es the signiﬁ cance of
the relic chamber and the stupa. Tangcharoensab
(2004) and Lerdwimolsak ( 2008) conducted reviews
of the ancient structural system of stupas in Ayutthaya.
The foundation is primarily a mat foundation, com-
posed of both a solid foundation and load-bearing
strips with compacted material inside. Due to their
ready availability in the area, burnt clay bricks were
predominantly used, while laterite materials were uti-
lized sparingly. The bricks are approximately 14 –
18 cm wide, 28– 34 cm long, and 4 –7 cm thick. The
most common pattern of brick arrangement follows
a longwise alignment of bricks, alternating with
bricks laid in a shortwise alignment, similar to the
Flemish bond and common header bond patterns
commonly used today. The pattern does not specify
how many bricks are to be alternated, but rather con-
tinues uninterrupted to achieve the desired thickness
and strength of the wall. The upper structures above
the base level up to the top were built using bricks
in the pattern described previously to support the
weight. Some stupas were constructed with a solid
brick system while others had hollow spaces inside,
using a corbelling pattern with bricks overlapping by

The stupa is about 26 meters tall and has a base area
of about 160 square meters. The geometry of the stupa
was documented digitally using an image-based
photogrammetry technique which can create a 3D
model using images through the Structure from
Motion (SfM) algorithm (Snavely, Seitz, and Szeliski
2008). The 3D model of the point cloud and solid
model for ﬁnite element analysis are shown in Figure
13 (b). The model is composed of 11,315 linear tetra-
hedron elements with its base ﬁxed to the ground.
The brick-and-mortar components were modeled as
an equivalent linear-elastic isotropic and homo-
geneous material.
The modulus of elasticity was determined by tuning
the model such that the ﬁrst vibration period matched
with the result from the ﬁeld experiment by ambient
vibration test which was 0.358 s. It was found that
the e ﬀective elastic modulus for this vibration period
is about 450 MPa. The mass density in this study is
assumed to be 1,800 kg/m 3. Poisson ’s ratio of the
material plays a limited role in the analysis and a
typical value of 0.2 is assumed. The strengths of the
composite are assumed to be the lower bound value
of those reported in Wonganan et al. ( 2021), i.e. the
equivalent tensile and compressive strengths of the
composite are 0.19 and 1.90 MPa respectively.
The ﬁnite element model of the stupa was con-
structed using a damping ratio of 2%, which was deter-
mined through ambient vibration testing that yielded
values between 1% to 3%. The model was analyzed
using 60 vibration modes, considering cumulative
eﬀective mass (Chopra 2007) as calculated from the
vibration modes. Results showed that the ﬁrst few
modes had signiﬁ cantly lower e ﬀective mass com-
pared to a model of a building structure, mainly
because the majority of the mass of the stupa is
located at the bottom, unlike buildings with uniformly
distributed mass. For the stupa model, using 60 modes
resulted in a cumulative e ﬀective mass of approxi-
mately 90%, which is recommended for seismic analy-
sis of structures. Examples of mode shapes obtained
from the modal analysis of the ﬁrst two modes are
shown in Figure 14 (a) and 14 (b). The solid lines
show the values of the stupa, where the mass and
stiﬀness are high at the base and decrease with
height. The dashed lines show the values of the
tower model, where the mass and sti ﬀness are uni-
formly distributed throughout the height. From com-
parisons of the two models, it can be observed that
the lower part of the stupa has very little movement
compared to the upper part, which is more ﬂexible
and undergoes signiﬁ cant deformation.
To provide a vibration input that corresponds to the
limited criterion of 1 mm/s, the vertical ground
vibration records at Ayutthaya were scaled to achieve
a maximum amplitude of 1 mm/s, and the same
scaling factor was applied to the horizontal com-
ponents of the records. These three components
were then input at the base of the stupa model as
the ground excitations. The modal time-history analy-
sis of the structure subjected to ground motions was
carried out and the stresses in each part of the stupa
were investigated. Tensile and compressive principal
stresses were computed to identify the possible
failure of material at any location on the structure.

Assessment of vibration e ﬀects on historic
structures
Vibration intensity and acceptance criteria for
historic buildings
Generally, the recommended values of vibration
acceptance criteria for buildings are deﬁ ned in service-
ability limit states, which are the limit of the hairline or
minor cracking, spalling of paint or plaster, excessive
deﬂection, or accelerated aging (Bachmann et al.
1995). Most vibration criteria have been developed
from experience and therefore those criteria are
empirical in nature. The recommended values
depend on the type of excitation, frequency content,
and duration, as well as the position where the
vibration is considered. The limits for historic buildings
are always much lower than those for other types of
structures. The tolerable values vary from country to
country and no single set of criteria seems to satisfy
all requirements. It should be noted that the rec-
ommended criteria do not guarantee the absence of
damage, but reduce its probability of occurrence to
acceptably low levels. Bachmann et al. ( 1995)

b) b) The maximum vertical (particle) velocity at the

c) c) The maximum vertical velocity for especially
sensitive buildings and buildings of cultural and
historical value induced by tra ﬃc should not
exceed 1 mm/s (Bonder and Rundquist 1981).
In Thailand, the Pollution Control Department of
Thailand has enforced the standard on vibration cri-
teria for buildings (Pollution Control Department
2010) which was adapted from DIN 4150– 3 standard
(1999). According to the standard, the maximum vel-
ocity of vibrations at the foundation of historic build-
ings should not exceed 3 mm/s.
Based on the above example vibration criteria, the
most conservative criterion of 1.0 mm/s will be used
as the allowable vibration intensity in this study.
Figure 10 shows the maximum vibration intensity
measured along the distance from roads in Ayutthaya
(AYA) compared with other sites. Each data point rep-
resents the highest amplitude obtained from several
tests at the site. At AYA, the maximum velocity is
about 0.5 mm/s at 4 m from the roadside. The intensity
of traﬃc vibration in Ayutthaya observed in this work is
lower than the acceptance criteria for historic build-
ings. It is noted that the intensity of vibration is also
dependent on the condition of tra ﬃc such as
volume, speed, and type. The peaks in tra ﬃc-busy
areas such as in BKK and SPK could be harmful to
any vulnerable structure. However, those sites are
not heritage sites.
Finite element analysis
Although a criterion from peak particle velocity is
useful to establish a guideline of the permissible
vibration level, this parameter alone cannot predict
the damage response of a structure. Therefore, it is
desirable to perform an analysis of the structure in
addition to the comparison of vibration intensity to
the recommended criteria. This study further con-
ducted a dynamic analysis to evaluate the stress level
induced from vibration on the ancient structure by
performing 3D ﬁnite element analysis.
The structure used as an example in this analysis is
Wat Sam Pluem stupa which is shown in Figures 1 and
2. The construction history of the stupa is not well-
documented, but the Fine Arts Department ( 2000)
has speculated about its architectural style based on
the bell-shaped design of the stupa, which stands on
an octagonal base. This old-style stupa was con-
structed from bricks without the use of mortar,
similar to the early Ayutthaya period. It is estimated
that the stupa at Wat Sam Pluem was built in the four-
teenth century or earlier. After the relocation of the
capital city from Ayutthaya to Bangkok, many
temples in Ayutthaya were left abandoned, including
Wat Sam Pluem stupa. In 1937, the government
began focusing on revitalizing the province of Phra
Nakhon Si Ayutthaya and planning a new city so
many roads were built in the city. This resulted in the
demolition of many historic sites, but the Fine Arts
Department had registered the Wat Sam Pluem stupa
as a historical site, preventing its destruction. There-
fore, it became necessary to build a roundabout
around the stupa instead of demolishing it.
Wat Sam Pluem stupa underwent the ﬁrst recon-
struction after the restoration of Ayutthaya city. It
was then restored once again following a major
ﬂood in 2011. The Fine Arts Department expressed
concern over the historic sites that were submerged
for approximately a month. The condition of the
stupa before reconstruction was described in a recon-
struction report (Fine Art Department 2012) as having
deteriorated surfaces and cracks in the plaster. Weeds
were also found growing along the cracks in the
plaster and the brick walls. In addition, fungi and
lichen were found on the plaster surface around the

Naret Limsamphancharoen 1 and Qudeer Hussain 2
1Faculty of Engineering, Thammasat School of Engineering, Thammasat University, Bangkok, Thailand; 2Center of Excellence in
Earthquake Engineering and Vibration, Department of Civil Engineering, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand
ABSTRACT
This paper presents an assessment study of tra ﬃc-induced ground vibrations and their e ﬀects
on masonry-type historic structures in Ayutthaya Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site
in Thailand. The ﬁrst objective is to propose a practical prediction of the attenuation rate of
vibration for risk management of the monuments located along roadsides in the city. The
attenuation of vibration waves traveling from traﬃ c sources and the intensity of ground
vibrations were determined by in situ vibration measurement. The results from the
investigations in the Ayutthaya area were compared with those obtained from other sites
having di ﬀerent characteristics of subsoil classiﬁed by the average shear wave velocity (Vs).
It was found that the attenuation rates at a long distance from the source tend to be
dependent on soil property in terms of Vs of subsoils. The attenuation curves derived from
the regression analysis are proposed for risk management from the vibration of the heritage
site. The second objective is to assess the e ﬀects of traﬃ c vibrations on historic structures.
The highest amplitude observed in Ayutthaya was within the recommended vibration
criteria for historic buildings. In addition, ﬁnite element analysis of a 3D stupa model
revealed that the stresses resulting from the ground vibration records induced by tra ﬃc was
lower than the strength of ancient brick and mortar.

Introduction
Ground vibrations induced by tra ﬃc, subways, or con-
struction activities can be harmful to nearby structures
if the level of shaking is severe. This problem is more
pronounced in cases of weak and fragile structures
such as ancient remains. Among detrimental environ-
mental impacts, vibrations are always concerning to
inhabitants as a primary cause of the deterioration of
vulnerable structures. This could be attributed to the
fact that tremors are most perceptible while other
eﬀects such as foundation settlement, temperature
change, relative humidity variations, or atmospheric
pollution are less immediately apparent so often
ignored. Moreover, problems of vibration in a city
often play a key role in the controversy over heritage
conservation and urban development. Lack of infor-
mation on vibration intensity and its e ﬀect can be a
cause of the problems. Therefore, it is necessary to
examine the potential impact of vibrations on histori-
cal structures to develop an appropriate conservation
plan. According to the theoretical principles of conser-
vation, the primary objective of interventions on fragile
ancient structures is to minimize the impact of
vibrations while preserving their authenticity and orig-
inal condition as much as possible. This requires
conducting a thorough study of the problem and the
structural behavior towards vibrations. This include
monitoring the severity of the vibration and prediction
of structural response using dynamic analysis to ident-
ify the weaknesses and vulnerable areas. This detailed
analysis will help determine the level of intervention
required to preserve the original condition.
Characteristics of a ground vibration depend on
several factors such as types of excitation, properties
of soil media in which vibration waves propagate,
and direction and distance from the source. In the
past few years, vibration monitoring for assessment,
mitigation, and control for heritage sites as well as art-
works has been implemented for problems caused by
a variety of sources (for example, Henningsson 2018;
Karanikoloudis et al. 2020; Yang et al. 2020). Tra ﬃc-
induced ground vibration is also a major threat to heri-
tage sites. It is generated from multiple excitation
sources, which are random in speed, frequency, ampli-
tude, and direction of wave propagation. The vibrations
cause stress waves to propagate outward from the
source in all directions. The propagation characteristics
of the wave depend mainly on characteristics of
vibration at the source, distance from the source, and
soil characteristics. In general, the intensity of the
wave decreases with the distance from the source

Attenuation rate of tra ﬃc vibration
In this work, the attenuation rate is deﬁ ned as the ratio
of the wave amplitude at the far location from the
source divided by the amplitude at the closer location.
It is an important parameter to characterize the decay-
ing rate of vibration and estimate the intensity of
vibration at a distance from roads. This study calculates
the attenuation rate of the wave traveling from the
traﬃc source from the vibration amplitudes measured
from sensors and discusses the results with the dis-
tance perpendicular to the tra ﬃc direction. For
example, in Figure 7 (a), the horizontal axis plots the
amplitude detected at sensor number 1 and the verti-
cal axis is the amplitude of the same wave detected at
sensor number 2, as referred to the sensor number in
Figure 4 . The attenuation rate from these sensors is
the slope of the straight line obtained from regression
analysis of data points. Figure 7 (a) indicates that the
amplitude at the second sensor reduces to about
84% of the value at the ﬁrst sensor. The results from
others pairs are presented in the same form in
Figures 7 (b) to 7 (f). The slope of each graph is less
than unity and decreases as the distance from the
source increases. In summary, Figure 8 shows the
plot of the attenuation rate against distance. The
results from Ayutthaya are compared with those
from other areas having di ﬀerent soil conditions. The
markers are the average ratio obtained from the
several tests and the broken lines show the tendency
of data of each site.

(BKK), and Samutprakarn (SPK). CRI exhibits the fastest
attenuation, which is corresponding to its highest Vs30
among all sites. From Figure 8, a simple prediction of

Site characteristics of the studied area
This study focuses on the sites in Ayutthaya historic park
(named AYA1 to AYA3) and extends the investigations
for comparison in neighboring cities having diﬀ erent
soil conditions, which are Pathumthani (PTE), Bangkok
(BKK), Samutprakarn (SPK), and Chiangrai (CRI). The
geotechnical properties of sedimentary materials vary
from site to site. The sites in AYA, PTE, BKK, and SPK
are situated on a large lower plain underlain by soft
clay deposits where the thickness of sediments
gradually increases from the north of the plain (AYA)
to the delta river in the south (SPK). The site in CRI is
on a ﬂuvial plain consisting of clay and sand sediments
and it is anticipated to be sti ﬀer than other sites. To
characterize the geotechnical properties related to
wave propagation of each site, the study considers
the shear wave velocity (Vs), the velocity at which
shear waves propagate, to represent the elastic shear
modulus, density, and dynamic sti ﬀness of the sedi-
ments. Sites with higher Vs have more sti ﬀ soils.
The technique to determine Vs proﬁ les employed is
the array microtremor observation, which appears as
an economical and practical method (Okada 2003).
The fundamental principle of this method is to
measure small-amplitude ground vibrations through
an array microtremor observation. This technique
involves recording ambient waves on the ground
using a set of sensors placed at speciﬁ ed intervals.
This study applied the Centerless Circular Array (CCA)
method, as proposed by Cho et al. ( 2006), which
employs microtremor sensors arranged in a circular
array. The vertical component of surface waves was
recorded for a su ﬃcient period to obtain a set of
signals that represents the natural wave traveling in
the soil layers. This is used to determine the phase vel-
ocity of the microtremor wave that passes through the
sensors. The analysis of the data using the CCA method
involves identifying the characteristics of the phase
velocity by analyzing the relationship between the vel-
ocity of the measured wave and the distance between
the sensors. This allows for the calculation of the phase
velocity for diﬀerent frequencies, which represents the
dispersive characteristics of the wave components. The

Traﬃc vibration measurement
The main equipment used in the vibration measure-
ment is a set of 3-axis sensors to record the ground
vibration in form of the velocity of motion and a
data recorder. The resolution of the analog-to-
digital converter is 24 bits with maximum converting
speed of 50 kHz, and maximum input voltage of
2.5 V. The sensitivity is 1 V/(cm/s). All sensors are con-
nected to the data acquisition unit through cables.
The system can measure velocity on the scale of
micro-m/s and the maximum scale is ± 2.5 cm/s.
The objective is to acquire surface waves under
normal tra ﬃc conditions at the site of study, and
examine their attenuation while traveling from the
source. In Figure 4 , the sensors are arranged perpen-

straight line, while Figure 5 shows the sensors
placed at a particular site. The sensor has three com-
